doc.title: Alvin Queen interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, August 23, 1997 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Horace Silver auditions and the loss of real bands
summary: Queen says Silver tests tempo discipline and that young players lack big-band experience of sounding as one.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Yeah. America, I love to work here, if the people are looking for what’s correct. My music is not about a challenge. My music is about reality. That’s it. So if they look for a drummer with twenty drums and red lights flashing in there, hey, you know, you’re not going to get the drum from me. You’re not going to get this big show type of thing, that’s not going to happen. The media and the market, I don’t know what it has done. But games I don’t play. I play some music and that’s it. But it’s not a challenge, and the young guy, a lot of the young musicians look at the music as a freeway or highway or something. Who plays the fastest? But remember one thing. When you do an audition with Horace Silver, it’s who can stay here [rhythmic finger snapping]. And every time you get a young musician right there, it falls apart. He hasn’t learned to stay there. That’s the trick. The trick is the discipline of how long and how constant you can keep that, to that degree. That’s the trick. That’s Horace. Horace’s got a way, he’ll say, “Uh huh, now I’m going to spot check this guy, I know what to do, count one — two — one two three.” And if that tempo falls apart he’ll say, “You’re not the one for the job.” That means the © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

young ones can play fast or too slow. Never like [scats]. And that’s the problem. That was one of the problems, man, was that they didn’t have enough experience with the Basies and the Duke Ellingtons and they don’t have those real bands anymore that teach you how to sound as one horn, not as many. Four horns as one.
It’s not something that’s around enough that you can absorb it.
That’s what’s so sad. But the market doesn’t keep it around. That’s what it is.
